class_id: a spec restates a schema constraint from memory, the schema later changes, and a whole workstream is justified by the stale copy
feature: any design document that quotes a limit the code or database actually owns — a column precision, a rate cap, a timeout, a size ceiling, a retention window — and then reasons from the quoted number rather than from the source
symptom: a spec needs to argue about a limit, so it writes the limit into a table. The number is right on the day it is written. Later the schema is widened, or was never what the author remembered, and nothing re-checks the copy because a document is not code and no test reads it. Work is then SIZED and JUSTIFIED from the stale number: a migration is planned, a repair tool is scoped, an owner is asked to approve a not-cleanly-reversible change. Nobody queries the live column, because the spec looks authoritative and quoting it feels like evidence. The tell is that the justification chain never touches the database: 'the spec says the column is numeric(15,2), therefore it overflows at X, therefore we must convert.' Each arrow is valid and the first premise was never measured. The generic test costs one query: before any work justified by a stated limit, read the limit from the thing that enforces it.
first_seen: 2026-09-21 — IPODhan item 11 (OD-20 crore conversion). The spec's §5.2 capacity table states rupee columns are `numeric(15,2)` (ceiling about 10 lakh crore) and uses that to argue Saudi Aramco at Rs 2.5 lakh crore would sit at a quarter of the ceiling — tight enough to motivate converting five columns to crore, a data migration the spec itself calls its own release and not cleanly reversible. Measured on the live database: all five columns are `numeric(18,2)`, ceiling Rs 1,00,00,00,000 crore. Aramco uses 0.025% of it — one four-thousandth, not one quarter. India's largest (Hyundai, Rs 27,870 cr) uses 0.0028%; the biggest row we hold (NSE, Rs 26,579.64 cr) uses 0.0027%. Postgres accepts the Aramco value in `numeric(18,2)` directly, verified. The owner had asked this exact question earlier — 'will the current field length hold the world's largest IPO? if yes there is no need to change it' — and the answer, from the schema rather than the spec, is yes with a factor of 4,000 to spare. I repeated the spec's 15,2 to the owner before reading `packages/shared/src/db/schema.ts`; the owner caught it by re-asking.
fix_prs: the immediate correction is to the SPEC, not the schema: §5.2's precision table now states numeric(18,2) with the measured headroom, and the conversion's capacity justification is withdrawn. The durable remedy is narrower than 'keep docs in sync', which never happens: a spec that quotes a limit names the OWNER of that limit next to it (`packages/shared/src/db/schema.ts:287`), so a reader can check in one step, and any work justified by the limit re-reads it from the owner as its first action rather than citing the document.
detection_check: none built. The cheap one is a test that parses capacity claims of the shape `numeric(P,S)` out of the design docs and asserts each against `information_schema.columns` for the named table.column — it is a small regex plus one query, and it would have failed the day the spec and schema diverged. Worth noting what made this findable at all: the owner asked the same question twice. The first time I answered from the spec; the second time I measured. A question re-asked is a signal that the first answer was thin, and is cheaper to act on than any check listed here.
